  • Artists who donate their own works to museums and galleries in the UK should receive tax breaks according to a newly introduced report published on Wednesday (18 November) focused on boosting cultural philanthropy.
  • The idea is one of a number of “tax enabling” proposals put forward by the think tank, The Cultural Policy Unit (CPU), which stresses in the report, “A National Strategy for Cultural Philanthropy”, that philanthropy “should be treated as both an urgent [UK] strategic priority and a deliberate instrument of cultural policy”.
  • The funding environment for culture has changed fundamentally, argues CPU which adds that “public finances have tightened considerably over the last 15 years, government funding for the arts has declined and self-generated income, while a key area, has not succeeded in plugging the widening gap.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artists who donate their own works to museums and galleries in the UK should receive tax breaks according to a newly introduced report published on Wednesday (18 November) focused on boosting cultural philanthropy.

The idea is one of a number of “tax enabling” proposals put forward by the think tank, The Cultural Policy Unit (CPU), which stresses in the report, “A National Strategy for Cultural Philanthropy”, that philanthropy “should be treated as both an urgent [UK] strategic priority and a deliberate instrument of cultural policy”.

The funding environment for culture has changed fundamentally, argues CPU which adds that “public finances have tightened considerably over the last 15 years, government funding for the arts has declined and self-generated income, while a key area, has not succeeded in plugging the widening gap.”.

In a wide-ranging set of recommendations, the report also suggests establishing a King’s Philanthropy Medal for Culture and setting up a national cultural “match-and-seed funding” programme with a regional focus.

Alison Cole, the director of the CPU and former editor of The Art Newspaper, says: “While the arts funding environment has changed dramatically in recent years, the philanthropic landscape has hardly kept pace let alone filled the gap with the UK lagging far behind the incentives offered by many of our European and US counterparts. We need a new national strategy that not only identifies the opportunities and need, but also thrives on a spirit of creative collaboration and mutual respect.”.

Recent findings suggest that artists who donate their own works to qualifying cultural institutions should receive tax recognition based on independent valuation, claims the think tank. Other tax-based recommendations include protecting charitable giving through inheritance planning—which means simplifying inheritance tax rules—and providing clearer rules around VAT.

Industry observers note that charles Saumarez Smith, who previously led the National Gallery, National Portrait Gallery and the Royal Academy of Arts, told The Art Newspaper that the report is “sensible”. “I particularly appreciated the information as to how other countries encourage philanthropy, not just the US,” he claims. “The biggest matter seems to me to be the lack of clarity round the existing systems, including, for example, around inheritance. How many people, even within cultural institutions, knows how this operates?”.

Industry observers note that the CPU acknowledges that Britain has a strong philanthropic tradition, arguing that its potential for cultural giving remains unrealised. Gift Aid, Acceptance in Lieu and the Cultural Gifts Scheme have all delivered real benefits but these schemes should be enhanced so that donors are more aware of their benefits, the report claims.

UK incentives are “broadly generous, but they are structured very differently from overseas models,“ according to the report. “The practical result is that British donors give quietly and anonymously, while the US and other systems reward public foundations and naming opportunities.”.

Kate Rolfe, a cultural strategy consultant, says: "Art organisations need to work with philanthropists who are inspired by the organisational vision and share their values and priorities, ensuring that the museum can stay focused on its purpose, vision and audiences." She believes corporate donations need to be reincentivised, as these often "lead to really creative partnerships based on shared audiences and values". Rolfe founded The Revels Office, a strategic audience and commercial development consultancy for the culture sector.

“Focused giving” may be partly the answer says the CPU, as evidenced by the Domani project at the National Gallery in London with £375m secured from Crankstart, the charitable foundation of Sir Michael Moritz and his wife Harriet Heyman, and the Julia Rausing Trust for a new Modern art wing. “The real transformation needs to be across the country and not just in the capital,” adds Cole.

The Associated Press is moving eight photo editor positions to India today, in a move condemned by unions.

Recent findings suggest that the roles are at the moment carried out in the United States, but today is their last day. The offshoring follows similar moves this summer, when AP laid off 20 video production jobs in the U.S. and moved them to its hub in Noida, India.

“AP is at it again,” the AP News Guild wrote on X last week. “The News Media Guild learned Monday that AP will offshore eight photo positions after already gutting its U.S. video production team.”.

In a statement, the News Media Guild president Kimberlee Krusei called AP’s move “union busting.”.

“Fewer people, fewer communities being covered, and less news. That’s the impact of today’s decision,” says Krusei. “AP’s newsgathering has gone beyond ‘lean’ to leaving many coverage areas abandoned. The remaining journalists are asked to do the impossible and it reveals.”.

The Guild says that far from just picking photos taken by AP photographers, the editors provide direction, guide the photographers, correct essential information, and scrutinize images for alterations.

“They bring decades of local knowledge, news judgment and connections. They negotiate with outside photographers to buy the rights to photos — a now essential part of covering breaking news.”.

One of the affected photo editors, Pablo Salinas, who is based in Fresh York, says that he went above and beyond in 2019 when he obtained the rights to a shocking photo of a drowned father and daughter lying face down in the Rio Grande River.

According to recent reports, “That was a picture that I don’t think any other photo editor would have been able to get,” indicates Salinas. “Because it wasn’t ours, I scoured social media and found it and got in touch with the photographer. And she reluctantly gave us permission to use it.”.

The photo went viral and became part of the story about the border crisis.

“AP benefits from having photo editors that are local to where the news is being produced,” says AP photographer Matt Rourke.

“It’s a partnership,” adds Salinas. “The kind of partnership you lose when you sacrifice these jobs to save a few dollars.”.

In a recent development, photo editors are intimately involved in the biggest stories of the day. They might be working closely with local photographers to move hundreds of shots illustrating crucial election results. Or securing the rights to sensitive images that convey difficult news. AP’s Pablo Salinas went in front of the camera to talk about the partnership that’s lost when news leaders sacrifice jobs like his. An AP spokesperson tells TheWrap that the agency is respecting and following the collective bargaining agreement.

“This is part of the changes we announced over the summer to significantly scale our visual production capabilities at our fresh hub in Noida, India, where we have added dozens of talented journalists to our global news organization,” the spokesperson indicates.

The AP notes that its hub in Noida will soon employ nearly 100 video producers and photo editors.

Turner Duckworth rebuilt the Maker's Mark brand identity around its red wax, casting Star Hill Farm materials into marks that tell the story.

According to recent reports, the bottle does the talking. Turner Duckworth kept the hand-dipped red top exactly where it belongs, at the center of the system, then built a whole language out of it. Wheat stalks, oak rings and native flora from Star Hill Farm were dipped and cast in the same red wax, so the marks that carry the brand are literal pieces of the place. Against a Wheat Cream ground, the red reads as one loud note in a quiet room, with Printmaker's Black holding the type steady.

Sources indicate that the type comes from a person, not a library. Co-founder Margie Samuels shaped the original bottle, and the studio recreated her handwriting as a custom typeface with Nick Cooke at G-Type. Hundreds of characters, contextual alternates and ligatures keep it feeling handwritten rather than set, and her voice runs through the labels, menus and posters in a flowing, wax-like hand.

Layouts stay plain on purpose. A letterhead puts the Samuels family's SIV mark at the center and the distillery address in the corner, so place sits at the heart of every sheet. Type stays large and calm, with room around it, and the wordmark does its work without decoration.

The palette is the bottle, remembered in three tones. Wheat Cream is the ground, true to the label. Printmaker's Black carries the type. Wax Red does the rest, in finish and in form: powder-coated metal, glazing and varnish applied to objects with smooth, flowing shapes. The same red runs across mugs, folders, books and table tents, so every object in the world feels dipped from the same pot.

Sources indicate that scott Grummett photographed the world at Star Hill Farm in warm cream tones and natural light, with touches of glossy wax red. The pictures tell the slower story behind the liquid: hand-rotated barrels, hand-cut labels, hand-dipped bottles, and the land that gives it flavour.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A drone operator filmed English soccer team Manchester United’s first training session with new coach Mauricio Pochettino and shared the “unethical” footage on YouTube.

Pochettino officially left the U.S. men’s national soccer team (USMNT) to become head coach of English Premier League club Manchester United. On Thursday, he oversaw his first training session with Man United’s first-team squad ahead of Sunday’s Premier League game against Liverpool at the club’s Carrington training ground.

It has been revealed that however, a drone operator who runs the YouTube account CC Overview — which describes itself as sharing “drone footage of construction at football stadia and events affecting our environment” — flew his aerial device over the facility during Pochettino’s first training session. He then posted a 12-minute segment on YouTube on Thursday.

According to a report by The Athletic, Pochettino and his players, who were split into three groups, were identifiable in the aerial footage, which amassed over 600,000 views on YouTube. The footage highlighted Pochettino leading a training session with one group of players, while his assistant Jesus Perez oversaw two separate groups. The video, filmed at United’s Carrington training base, also captured audio of the YouTuber apparently controlling the drone saying “let’s get closer,” before zooming in on the new head coach.

Sources indicate that the drone operator has since apologized for a “total error in judgment.” He claims the aerial footage was legal under U.K. drone laws but has removed the “unethical” video from YouTube.

“A total error of judgement on my part led to me filming some of the Man United training session at Carrington, whilst the flight was legal in terms of drone laws I fully accept it was unethical on my part,” the drone operator writes in a post on YouTube.

According to recent reports, the drone operator describes aiming to film Pochettino in the club’s training kit for the first time, but adds he had no intention of recording a “meaningful training session.” The YouTuber says he was operating under an incorrect assumption that it was open to media outlets. He also insists he acted independently and was not working on behalf of Liverpool or any other football club.

“I would like to apologize to Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino and the players for my actions and sincerely hope those actions do not affect the outcome of any match,” the drone operator indicates.

Man United prohibits the use of drones at its Carrington training facility, where signs warn that anyone operating a drone could face civil action or prosecution.

In the U.K., capturing aerial footage using drones is permitted provided operators comply with Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) safety regulations, as well as privacy and data protection laws.

CAA guidance on privacy for drone use details: “If you use these devices where people can expect privacy, such as inside their home or garden, you’re likely to be breaking data protection laws.” It adds that drone operators should “let people know before you start recording or taking pictures”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Syrian photographer has finally been reunited with his personal photo archive more than a decade after hiding it behind a wall he built during the country’s war.

Photographer Ahmed al-Bekkar fled Syria more than a decade ago, seeking refuge in Turkey amid widespread destruction, looting, and attacks by the terrorist group ISIS (Daesh) and forces loyal to Syria’s now-topled Assad regime, according to a report by Anadolu Agency.

‘Every piece of paper has a history, every page holds a memory’.

🇸🇾 Syrian photographer Ahmed al-Bekkar recovers personal archive in Raqqa after more than a decade.

● Bekkar, 66, sealed his library before fleeing war to protect books, photographs and personal documents.

● He sought refuge in Türkiye amid attacks by Daesh (ISIS) and forces of ousted Syrian regime.

— Anadolu English (@anadoluagency) November 19, 2026.

Before leaving Syria, Bekkar built a wall to conceal the entrance to his personal library in the northern city of Raqqa, hoping to protect his extensive photographic archive. The archive contains approximately 3,000 printed photographs of Raqqa, as well as a much larger digital collection documenting historical sites, cities, and markets across Syria.

During his decade in Turkey, the now 66-year-old photographer continued his photographic work, helping establish the House of Migrants association and the Turkish-Arab Art House. Although Bekkar spent productive years doing photography in the Turkish capital of Istanbul, he says nothing could replace his hometown in Syria.

Anadolu Agency reports that Bekkar returned to Raqqa this year and reopened the library he had concealed behind the wall more than a decade earlier. The photographer describes watching the bricks being removed one by one from the wall as an emotional experience, having long dreamed of setting foot inside his archive again.

“Every piece of paper has a history, every page holds a memory. I spent time and effort obtaining and preserving every document,” the photographer tells the news outlet. “I feel that those days are preserved in these papers, whose owners are no longer with us, but which have remained behind.”.

According to recent reports, bekkar recalled growing up across from an old mosque in Raqqa, where the surrounding historical buildings inspired his interest in photography and Syria’s cultural heritage. Since returning to his hometown, Bekkar has revisited historical sites he photographed years earlier to document them now.

Stedelijk Museum appoints Krist Gruijthuijsen as fresh director

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam has confirmed that the Dutchman Krist Gruijthuijsen will take over as its new director from July 2027.
  • Moving from Finland, where he has since 2025 been director of the Espoo Museum of Modern Art (EMMA), he stated he wants to bring an outsider’s perspective and a focus on how the modern city connects with the world.
  • Industry observers note that “The Stedelijk museum’s strength is in bringing large and Modernist exhibitions to the Netherlands,” he tells The Art Newspaper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam has confirmed that the Dutchman Krist Gruijthuijsen will take over as its new director from July 2027.

Moving from Finland, where he has since 2025 been director of the Espoo Museum of Modern Art (EMMA), he stated he wants to bring an outsider’s perspective and a focus on how the modern city connects with the world.

Industry observers note that “The Stedelijk museum’s strength is in bringing large and Modernist exhibitions to the Netherlands,” he tells The Art Newspaper. “People go to the Rijksmuseum for Rembrandt and to the city [Stedelijk] museum to understand how Amsterdam has developed, to understand Modernism through the lens of art and design.”.

The Stedelijk Museum enjoyed success last year with an Anselm Kiefer show—organised with the neighbouring Van Gogh Museum—and an exhibition of work by the Dutch photographer Erwin Olaf, increasing annual ticket revenue compared to 2024 by almost a quarter, to €10.8 million. Its current Yayoi Kusama show has been extended to the end of January due to its popularity.

It has been revealed that this success stands out against a backdrop of Dutch museums reporting financial pressure and a fall in visits compared to pre-pandemic levels. The Rijksmuseum’s most recent annual report describes internal discussions that took place about the fact visitor numbers fell 4% in 2025 to 2.3 million, while the Rembrandt House Museum recently warned that rising tourist taxes will damage cultural tourism.

According to recent reports, but Gruijthuijsen said he is more interested in variety than visitor records. “I’m not a visitor numbers director,” he notes. “It is quality rather than quantity: what we need economically, and the rest is a plus. It is very difficult these days because people only choose what they know. My goal is first and foremost to support artists and art.”.

Gruijthuijsen takes over from Rein Wolfs, who has been the director since 2019.

Industry observers note that from one of the first exhibitions to establish Van Gogh’s work in 1905 to experimental indicates of the 1960s, the Stedelijk Museum created an international reputation for contemporary art, which Gruijthuijsen wants to make relevant today. “The DNA of the city museum is a modern day and global perspective—trying to find connections,” he says.

From the Finns, he will also bring an vital lesson in terms of improving diversity and tackling under-represented subjects, he states: “Less talking, more doing.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pentagram drew a full custom alphabet for Storefront Gala 2026, turning the Oyster Bar sign into loud, blocky, crayon-bright type.
  • Recent findings suggest that the gala took over the Grand Central Oyster Bar on September 28, honoring artist Mel Chin, arts leader Deana Haggag, and the architecture firm SO-IL.
  • In a recent development, the answer is a custom display typeface with a full set of letters and numerals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pentagram drew a full custom alphabet for Storefront Gala 2026, turning the Oyster Bar sign into loud, blocky, crayon-bright type.

Recent findings suggest that the gala took over the Grand Central Oyster Bar on September 28, honoring artist Mel Chin, arts leader Deana Haggag, and the architecture firm SO-IL. Anyone who has eaten under those Guastavino vaults knows the sign on the wall. Rudolph de Harak packed its letters tight, rimmed them in heavy black outlines, and filled them with colors straight out of a crayon box. Against wood paneling and old tile, it has always looked like the one guest in the room who came to have fun. Pentagram started from a simple question: what would the rest of that alphabet look like?

In a recent development, the answer is a custom display typeface with a full set of letters and numerals. Strokes run broad, corners clip short, and counters turn angular. The O is an octagon with a diamond punched through its middle, and that shape sets the rules for every other character. Blue, green, yellow, orange, red, and purple take turns filling the forms.

Storefront Gala 2026 appears in compact stacks and stepped arrangements, with rotated numerals adding an unexpected twist. Letters meet along their black outlines and lock into continuous compositions that feel assembled from colorful building blocks. A smaller sans serif organizes the event information around these expressive forms, holding the honorees, the venue, and the date in quiet lines above the noise.

According to recent reports, the system runs across digital announcements, posters, a folded program, screen graphics, and embroidered caps. Some pieces set the colored letters on white, while others flood the ground with a single saturated color and let the type push back. The folded program carries the full stack in a run of blue, green, yellow, orange, red, and purple, with the small sans serif keeping the facts straight at the top of the sheet.

The caps are the most tactile piece of the set, the lettering stitched small across white, green, and pale blue cotton. An orange sign stands on the tiled floor, and the word SALOON stretches across a wood doorway in the same blocky letters, proof the alphabet holds its shape from a poster down to a doorway. Pentagram has designed identities for Storefront since 2012, and this one plays the longest with the room it was made for.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Heffel Fine Art Auction House held its marquee autumn evening sales on Wednesday (18 November) in Toronto, attracting a packed house of bidders and spectators to the city’s swank Yorkville district and generating C$14.4m ($10m) in sales, works by Canadian masters taking top dollar. As things got underway, a Heffel representative noted that any US tariffs were “the responsibility of the buyer”, a reflection of these often-testy times.

“At a time of strong national pride, it is especially meaningful to see collectors celebrating Canada’s artistic achievements and our distinct national culture,” David Heffel, the auction house’s president, said at the end of the evening.

Heffel's evening auctions in Toronto on 18 November Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

Industry observers note that the back-to-back sales (41 lots of post-war and contemporary art followed by 47 works of Canadian, Impressionist and modern art) got off to a flying start when a watercolour by the Vancouver-born artist E.J. Hughes hammered for C$475,000 ($331,700)—nearly 12 times its high estimate. Titled Wharves at Chemainus (2000) and depicting the titular logging community on Vancouver Island, the painting is modest in size at 20in by 24in; with fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900).

Industry observers note that hughes had made waves at Heffel’s auctions last spring, when his Coastal Boats Near Sidney, BC realised a whoppingC$5.7m ($4.1m), including fees. Several more Hughes works were up for sale Wednesday night including two that significantly outperformer their estimates: The Hope River at Chilliwack, BC (1961), which took in C$253,250 ($176,800) with fees; and The Freighter “World Ares” at Crofton (1980), which hauled in C$229,250 ($160,000) including fees.

Emily Carr, Alert Bay (with Welcome Figure), around 1912 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

It has been revealed that the second sale’s cover lot, Emily Carr’s luminous canvas Alert Bay (with Welcome Figure) (around 1912), brought C$1.3m ($922,000) including fees, comfortably within its estimate. It was the only seven-figure result of the night. Some of the proceeds from its sale will benefit the Audain Art Museum in Whistler, British Columbia, where it was shown in the context of a major traveling exhibition of Carr’s work in 2019-20.

It has been revealed that A work on paper by the Carr, Music in the Trees (around 1935), topped its high estimate to achieve an impressive C$421,250 ($294,100) with fees. In all, six works by the Victoria-born artist were sold at Heffel on Wednesday night, fetching a combined, fee-inclusive total of C$2.5m ($1.7m).

Jean Paul Riopelle, Herbeuse, 1967 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

A handful of works by Jean Paul Riopelle were on offer during the post-war and contemporary portion of the night, generating around C$1.3m ($907,800) in sales. His large-scale, wintry abstraction Herbeuse (1967),proved particularly appealing. Swift bidding pushed it to around double its high estimate. With fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900). It was shown in the Carnegie International the year Riopelle painted it, and later in Paris, where the Montréal-born artist, a master of the palette knife, spent decades. The work with the highest estimate in the post-war and contemporary sale, Riopelle’s Brumaire (1953), was expected to bring between C$1.5m and C$2m, but failed to sell.

Recent findings suggest that among the night’s other big-ticket items was Paul-Émile Borduas’s oil painting Empâtement (1957), from the artist’s black-and-white period—and punctuated with splashes of red. It realised C$841,250 with fees ($587,400), easily topping its high estimate of C$500,000. It had been acquired directly from the artist by London’s Arthur Tooth & Sons gallery in 1957 and, more recently, was in the collection of Québecois lyricist and songwriter Luc Plamondon.

Paul-Émile Borduas, Empâtement, 1957 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

According to recent reports, J.E.H. MacDonald’s oil sketch Magnetawan River Rapids (1912), a preparatory work for a major canvas that is in the collection of the Art Gallery of Hamilton, achieved C$451,250 with fees ($315,000), tripling its high estimate of C$150,000.

Sources indicate that arguably the surprise of the night was Ivan Eyre (1935-2022), who was long a professor at the University of Manitoba and is best known for his prairie landscapes. His intensely autumnal acrylic-on-canvas landscape Golden Rod (1981) realised C$391,250 with fees ($273,200), more than tripling its high estimate of C$120,000 while setting a newly introduced auction record for the artist. That record was smashed in turn just one lot later, when Eyre’s Yellow Wood (around 1995) realised C$481,250 with fees ($336,000), five times its high estimate of C$90,000.

Ivan Eyre, Golden Rod, 1981 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

The beloved William Kurelek, who was raised on a farm near Winnipeg, also made a splash.His snowy landscape painting I Knew How the Clouds Arise (1969), which was featured on the cover of the catalogue for the artist’s first retrospective in 1970, realised C$313,250 including fees ($218,700), just over its high estimate, while the evocative campfire scene Wiener Roast on My Father’s Farm (1974), exceeded expectations to sell for C$265,250 with fees ($185,200).

💡 Key Takeaways

  • For years, Adobe has incentivized photographers to contribute to its picture marketplace by dangling the carrot of a free subscription to Photoshop and other Adobe apps.
  • Robert Kneschke, a professional stock photographer based in Germany who runs the Daily Life of a Photo Producer blog, indicates that in 2020, a photographer needed 150 sales to unlock a free Adobe Photography plan, while 5,000 downloads would net them complete access to Creative Cloud.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Adobe will no longer offer complimentary Creative Cloud subscriptions to photographers who sell their work through Adobe Stock, replacing the scheme with discounts instead.

For years, Adobe has incentivized photographers to contribute to its picture marketplace by dangling the carrot of a free subscription to Photoshop and other Adobe apps.

Robert Kneschke, a professional stock photographer based in Germany who runs the Daily Life of a Photo Producer blog, indicates that in 2020, a photographer needed 150 sales to unlock a free Adobe Photography plan, while 5,000 downloads would net them complete access to Creative Cloud.

According to recent reports, but Adobe has recently made changes to its bonus program, changing the eligibility and prizes. Instead of offering full complimentary access, Adobe is offering a 70% discount on Creative Cloud Pro to the first 500 contributors who generate 6,500 downloads and submit over 1,000 newly introduced images.

The 70% discount is also on offer to the first 500 contributors who “have 10 or more datasets and maintain high quality standards.” It’s not entirely clear what a dataset is from a photographer’s perspective. On its website, Adobe describes it as a “storage and management construct for a collection of data, typically a table, that contains a schema (columns) and fields (rows).”.

There’s also a 40% discount on offer for Creative Cloud Pro for the first 10,000 contributors who generate more than 2,500 sales as well as submitting over “100 pieces of unique content.”.

Sources indicate that the above criteria must be met from September 22, 2026, to March 12, 2027. The codes will be handed out in April.

Adobe will still provide full complimentary access to Creative Cloud Pro to photographers who are “actively commissioned to create content and/or require Adobe tools to fulfill project requirements.”.

Writing on his blog, Kneschke calls the changes a “clear step backward” while speculating that the datasets are for AI training purposes.

Sources indicate that “A gift has become a discount voucher,” Kneschke indicates. “Along with the lower royalties, this is further evidence that Adobe is cutting costs at the expense of photographers.”.

Earlier this year, PetaPixel reported on Gerald Carter, the owner of Diversity Photos, and his fight with Adobe after he discovered that the firm trained its AI image generator Firefly on his entire photo library.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Smith & Diction rebuilt the PHS brand identity around a Bloom logo, with three plants growing from the letters and Philadelphia grid underneath.

The old mark was a tree in a circle, and it said too little about an organization that does far more than plant trees. The Pennsylvania Horticultural Society tends gardens and parks across the Philadelphia region and runs the Flower Show. The new mark keeps the letters PHS as the foundation and grows three plants out of them, each drawn by Summer McClure to fit a Philadelphia city block. In deep green and burgundy on cream, mint, and sky blue, with dozens of colors in the palette, the identity looks like a garden because it behaves like one: every visit highlights something new.

The wordmark is custom, built to hold the plants like roots hold a stem. The supporting type comes from the societyâs own archive: old exhibition posters that were beautiful and hardworking, no frills, just type. Caslon Doric leads, with the confidence and clean legibility of classic newspaper headlines, and ES Park backs it up, a slab serif with geometric moments and measured softness.

Industry observers note that underneath it all sits William Pennâs original city grid. The studio baked the grid into the logo itself, then extended it through every print layout, matching the grid to the width of the flowers. Like beds in a garden, the structure keeps everything in place while each layout keeps its own personality. The mark never sits still: Henrique Barone hand-drew every frame of the plants growing, and Justin Lawes made a version that sways with the breeze.

According to recent reports, this is a brand made to be held, not just seen. The studio printed a 42-page brand book, made a matte gold lapel pin of the mark, and built a flip book that reveals the logo growing frame by frame. They matched paper tones to nearly every brand color, so the team can print in-house and stay on brand. The book cover carries the Bloom logo in dark green on mint, with an orange seal.

The floral illustrations do more than decorate. Each one stands for a part of the organization: a flower in a cocktail glass for the Pop Up Gardens, a leafy radish for the community gardens, an oak leaf for the Healthy Neighborhoods program, a branching tree for the McLean Library. The library also gives the 2027 Philadelphia Flower Show its own peony mark, while Bre Furlongâs photographs of 18 flowers, including the tulip the studio calls the Ballerina, carry the ICONIC theme in Herbus type.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that three photographers have sued the St. Paul Police Department in Minnesota over its alleged use of chemical munitions against them during an ICE raid, with their own photographs documenting the incident.

Warning: The following photos contains content that some may find upsetting.

It has been revealed that aaron Nesheim, a photographer for Sahan Journal, MPR News photojournalist Kerem Yücel, and freelance photographer Timothy Evans filed the lawsuit against the St. Paul Police Department on Tuesday. The photographers accuse officers of firing pepper balls at them, pepper-spraying them at close range, and deploying tear gas against them while they were covering a demonstration.

Recent findings suggest that the lawsuit stems from an incident on November 25 last year, when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents attempted to arrest a man at his home in the Payne-Phalen neighborhood of St. Paul, Minnesota. A growing crowd of protesters gathered outside the property as federal agents attempted to detain the man.

Recent findings suggest that nesheim, Yücel, and Evans arrived at the scene to document the protest. All three photographers carried large professional cameras and wore press passes around their necks. Evans also wore a ballistic vest labeled “PRESS.”.

According to a report by the Minnesota Reformer, St. Paul police officers also responded to the scene. After ICE agents left with the detainees, protesters demanded that local police leave as well. As the officers withdrew, they fired pepper balls and used pepper spray and tear gas against both protesters and photojournalists.

According to court documents, an officer pepper-sprayed Yücel at close range while he was photographing the scene. The lawsuit says that the photographer inhaled and swallowed the chemicals. Other officers fired pepper balls at Yücel, striking him in the neck, shoulders, and chest.

In a recent development, according to the complaint, the three photographers were standing together off to the side of the crowd, at least 10 feet from the nearest protesters and out of the way of law enforcement officers. Despite this, police allegedly fired pepper balls and launched tear gas at the photographers.

Recent findings suggest that all three photographers experienced irritation to their eyes and airways following exposure to the chemicals. Yücel struggled to breathe and was taken from the scene by ambulance. According to MPR News, Yücel was forced to put his jacket into a garbage bag to prevent the chemicals from affecting the crew and staff at Regions Hospital mentioned they could not admit Yücel into the main hospital because the chemical irritants on his body and clothing posed a safety risk to staff and other patients.

Evans suffered severe abdominal bruising after a pepper ball exploded inside his ballistic vest, while Nesheim was struck in the head by a police projectile. All three photojournalists required mental health treatment following the incident.

The photographers argue in their lawsuit that the St. Paul Police Department’s actions violated their rights under the First, Fourth, and Fourteenth Amendments of the U.S. Constitution and constituted assault and battery, among other violations. They are seeking damages, attorney’s fees, and a court order barring the St. Paul Police Department from engaging in further unconstitutional conduct against them.

It has been revealed that “The use of this tear gas, like the use of the pepper balls, was clearly meant as retaliation for plaintiffs’ exercise of their First Amendment rights,”attorney Kevin Riach writes. “The officers could not have been shooting at anyone other than Nesheim, Yücel and Evans, who were all clustered within several feet of one another.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Association of Photographers (AOP) has announced the 36 finalists for its 2026 AOP Open Awards, a competition celebrating still and moving images by professional and amateur photographers from around the world.

Sources indicate that now in its 20th year, the competition allows photographers of all experience levels to compete on equal terms. Sponsored by Capture One, Fujifilm UK, and Maxima, this year’s awards are divided into three formats: single image, series, and moving image.

It has been revealed that the finalists’ work will be exhibited at Fujifilm House of Photography in London from January 29 to March 14, 2027. The Gold and Silver winners will be unveiled at a private viewing on the evening of January 28.

The Best in Show winner will receive £1,250 ($1,600), while the Gold and Silver winners will take home £250 and £100, respectively. Additional prizes from the sponsors and AOP membership are also on offer.

The 36 shortlisted works cover a wide range of subjects, from LGBTIQ+ communities in the remote jungles of Suriname to Muslim women competing in Tbourida, an equestrian sport with roots in 16th-century battle tactics.

Other projects explore the tradition of workers, local clubs, and Sunday league teams playing football on London’s Hackney Marshes, alongside images of the game being played away from conventional pitches in Morocco. Elsewhere, photographers document the 40,000 Elvis impersonators and fans who descend on Porthcawl, a small seaside town in South Wales, for the world’s largest Elvis Presley festival.

The finalists also include a portrait of a woman continuing to run her family’s flower business in Kyiv throughout the war in Ukraine, portraits of national treasures David Hockney and Dame Judi Dench, and a visual ode to gratitude for skin.

All 36 finalist projects can be viewed on the AOP Awards website.

Industry observers note that the AOP Open Awards accept entries without categories or prescribed themes, leaving photographers free to submit work that is either personal or commissioned. The competition welcomes still photography, moving images, and creative uses of technology and innovation in work produced by a person. AI-generated images are not accepted, and all entries must have been created on or after January 1, 2025.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Werkligâs web design for Finnish energy firm Voltcore pairs Store Norske Skandia and Skandia Mono across foggy snow ridges and grid hardware.
  • It has been revealed that A snow-packed ridge fades into pale winter fog across Voltcoreâs opening screen, pushing the white headline down into the lower-left corner.
  • Werklig gives each typeface a strict job, and it doesnât blur the line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Werkligâs web design for Finnish energy firm Voltcore pairs Store Norske Skandia and Skandia Mono across foggy snow ridges and grid hardware.

It has been revealed that A snow-packed ridge fades into pale winter fog across Voltcoreâs opening screen, pushing the white headline down into the lower-left corner. Up top, thereâs no clutter. Just a spaced VOLTCORE wordmark on the left and four tiny monospaced links (About, Services, Team, Contact) pinned to the right edge. Helsinki studio Werklig designed the identity and site for the Finnish energy company, which develops grid-balancing, baseload, and hybrid power assets across the Nordics. Featured on Fonts In Use, the web design runs on two siblings from Skriftkompani: Store Norske Skandia and Store Norske Skandia Mono. Scroll past that frosty hero and photography drops away, leaving three oversized charcoal paragraphs under a tiny About us tag to explain why Nordic grids need weather-independent power in dark winters.

Werklig gives each typeface a strict job, and it doesnât blur the line. Store Norske Skandia carries headlines and statements, while Store Norske Skandia Mono handles navigation, eyebrows, and captions with the crisp cadence of an engineering log. That split sharpens in the three-column What we do grid below. Three desaturated vertical photographs sit side by side: ribbed ceramic substation insulators against grey sky, a lattice transmission tower half-swallowed by mist, and an overhead power-line switch silhouetted against stark white. Beneath every frame sits an identical three-step stack â a mono tag for Balancing, Baseload, or Hybrid, a proportional subhead, and a tight monospaced caption. No rounded cards or drop shadows get in the way, so the web design reads cleanly on a single scan.

Near the bottom, winter returns up close. A wind-carved snowdrift curves across the contact band in blue-grey shadow, holding white display copy above a full-width hairline rule and [email protected]. Directly underneath, a pale-grey footer splits into four monospaced columns for Voltcore Oyâs phone line, Helsinki street address, Business ID 3638975-9, and a Back to top arrow. Itâs plain operational typography, right down to the registry number. Then the bottom strip snaps to pure white, stretching a monumental black VOLTCORE wordmark edge to edge. That final scale jump flips the compact header mark into a stark closing band for the web design.

#92067. Tech Report: Christie’s tepid 21st-century sale caps week of blockbuster auctions in Fresh York

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1661 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Christie’s tepid 21st-century sale caps week of blockbuster auctions in Fresh York

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1661 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, wrapping up this autumn’s week of marquee evening sales in Latest York, Christie’s 21st-century auction on Thursday (19 November) proved rather lacklustre, bringing in $117.7m ($145.9m with fees).
  • Industry observers note that just five of the 56 lots offered Thursday night failed to sell, for a slim buy-in rate of 9%.
  • Roy Lichtenstein, Small Wall Explosion, 1965 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, wrapping up this autumn’s week of marquee evening sales in Latest York, Christie’s 21st-century auction on Thursday (19 November) proved rather lacklustre, bringing in $117.7m ($145.9m with fees). That tally fell short of Christie’s pre-sale expectations, which do not account for fees, and projected a total take in the range of $126m to $192m. It was also a lower result compared to the auction house’s last two equivalent sales in New York—namely the $132m ($162.6m with fees) generated across 42 lots last May, and the $99.5m ($123.5m with fees) brought by 45 lots one year ago.

Industry observers note that just five of the 56 lots offered Thursday night failed to sell, for a slim buy-in rate of 9%. Two lots were withdrawn at the last moment, including a Jeff Koons sculpture estimated to bring between $3m and $5m. Twenty-four lots were backed by third-party guarantees and nine were backed fully by house guarantees, representing around 59% of all the works offered. Auction records for three artists were broken over the course of the night.

Roy Lichtenstein, Small Wall Explosion, 1965 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

It has been revealed that business began with a bang at Christie’s Rockefeller Center salesroom: the first lot was Roy Lichtenstein’s Small Wall Explosion (1965), executed in porcelain enamel on steel and perforated steel relief to mimic the Ben-Day dot style from his paintings. It sold to a telephone bidder for $625,000 ($800,000 with fees). From an edition of six, it hailed from the collection of Antonio Homem Sonnabend, the adopted son of the late and legendary dealer and collector Ileana Sonnabend (1914-2007) and who ran his mother’s namesake gallery in its waning years. Antonio Homem died earlier this year, at age 86.

Another of the 19 Sonnabend lots from Sonnabend, Ashley Bickerton’s expansive wall relief Commercial Piece #3 (1990), covered with gallery and fashion-house logos and comprised of anodised aluminium, wood, leather, acrylic and rubber, sold for $120,000 ($153,600 with fees). Both the Lichtenstein and the Bickerton were backed by third-party guarantees.

Andy Warhol, Campbell's Soup Can (Turkey Noodle), 1962 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Price points for the Sonnabend trove zoomed higher with Andy Warhol’s iconicand hand painted Campbell’s Soup Can (Turkey Noodle) (1962), which sold for $7.3m ($9m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. Another Lichtenstein, the painting Large Spool (1963)—a razor-sharp depiction of the titular object that has been featured in multiple gallery and museum exhibitions—squeaked by on the tails of a third-party guarantee at $7m ($8.6m with fees) against an ambitious estimate of $10m to $15m.

Still in the Sonnabend lots, Jeff Koons’s toy-like Hulk (Friends) (2004-12), in polychromed bronze and standing nearly 6ft tall, found a new home for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees). And another Warhol, redolent with Hollywood celebrity, The Kiss (Bela Lugosi) (1963) in silkscreen ink on white paper, sold to another telephone bidder for $3.3m ($4.6m with fees).

A petite Jasper Johns oil painting on cardboard, Numbers (1957), measuring just 8.5in by 6in and rich in shades of grey, made $2.6m ($3.2m with fees). It was featured in the artist’s first solo exhibition at the Leo Castelli Gallery in 1958. Ileana Sonnabend acquired it from the Castelli Gallery in 1959, the same year of her divorce from Leo Castelli.

The Sonnabend group of 19 lots, including three examples of crucial 20th-century French decorative art—among them a Jean Prouvé Trapéze table from around 1956 that hit $1.3m ($1.6m with fees)—all in tallied $33.3m ($41.9m with fees), compared to Christie’s pre-sale expectations for the group of $35m to $55m.

Illustrious consignor names continued with works from the collection of the late Museum of Modern Art trustee and patron Agnes Gund sold to benefit the Gund Art Foundation. They included Robert Ryman’s immaculate, small, square all-over white composition Untitled (1961), which brought $2.9m ($3.6m with fees). Vija Celmins’s photorealist oil painting Untitled (Ocean) (1990), which featured in the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s traveling retrospective in 2018-2020, went for $5.7m ($7.1m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. It also was backed by a third-party guarantee.

Vija Celmins, Untitled (Ocean), 1990 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Gund acquired Alexander Calder’s hanging metal mobile The Eye in the Black (1963) from the Perls Galleries in Upcoming York in in 1967. On Thursday night it went to an online bidder for $2.8m ($3.5m with fees). Cindy Sherman’s Untitled Film Still #5 (1977), also widely exhibited and written about by major critics, sold for $320,000 ($409,6000 with fees). Gund had acquired it at Sotheby’s New York in November 2000 for a hammer price of $75,000.

Recent findings suggest that gund’s contemporary taste bordered on the encyclopaedic, as evidenced by an early Robert Rauschenberg work, Untitled (Gold Painting) (1953), in gold leaf on fabric and paper collage on canvas. The diminutive work, at 8in by 8in, fetched a sizeable sum, $1.7m ($2.1m with fees). Gund acquired it at Sotheby’s in Fresh York in May 1994 for a $55,000 hammer price.

A modestly scaled Lichtenstein work on paper in coloured pencil, graphite and paper collage, Artist’s Studio with Model (Study) (1974), sold to the art adviser Ralph DeLuca for $950,000 ($1.2m with fees).

Jim Nutt, Loom, 1999 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

It has been revealed that A standout from the Gund trove, a work she described as “my Mona Lisa”, was another modestly-scaled work, by Jim Nutt, founder of Chicago’s Hairy Who group. Titled Loom (1999) and measuring 15in by 14in, the portrait of a woman with a penetrating gaze set a newly introduced auction record for Nutt’s work when it more than doubled its high estimate of $350,000 and ultimately sold for $850,000 ($1m with fees). The ten lots sold to benefit Gund’s charitable foundation tallied $20.3m ($25.7m with fees), squarely within Christie’s pre-sale estimate of $16m to $24m.

Recent findings suggest that though not part of the Gund Art Foundation offerings, Alice Neel’s double portrait David and Catherine Saalfield (1982) hailed from Agnes Gund’s family and brought $1.6m ($2m with fees). Gund acquired it directly from the artist the year it was painted—not surprising since the sitters were her young adult children.

Alice Neel, David and Catherine Saalfield, 1982 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

The appeal of buying a piece of the legacy of storied dealers and collectors did not fare so well for a work that had belonged to the late gallerist Marian Goodman. Bidding on Gerhard Richter’s Abstraktes Bild (1990) stalled at $5.7m, against an estimate of $6m to $8m, and the lot failed to sell. As Richter’s longtime Upcoming York dealer, Goodman acquired the lushly surfaced squeegee painting directly from the artist and exhibited the painting in a gallery group show the year it was made. (A second Richter from another consignor fared better, with that somewhat larger Abstraktes Bild from 1991 bringing $7.6m, or $9.4m with fees.).

Among the works from more anonymous consignors, Richard Prince’s famous Nurse series made a splash when Everglade Nurse (2003), executed in acrylic and inkjet print on canvas, sold for $3.1m ($3.9m with fees). It last sold at Sotheby’s New York in November 2008 for $3.4m with fees, a rather flat return after 18 years.

Recent findings suggest that large-scale paintings destined to test living room wall space were also in evidence with Christopher Wool’s untitled black-and-white abstraction from 2009, measuring more than 8ft tall. It brought $2m ($2.5m with fees). George Condo’s more than 9ft-wide Double Heads in Blue and Silver (2014), realised $2.4m ($3m with fees). The Condo hailed from the collection of Stefan Edlis and his wife Gael Neeson, who donated 44 works cumulatively valued at more than $400m to the Art Institute of Chicago in 2015.

The top lot of the evening, unsurprisingly, was Jean-Michel Basquiat’s quirky and text-rich composition, Untitled (Leonardo and his Five Grotesque Heads) (1983), which hammered to another anonymous telephone bidder for $28m ($32.8m with fees) against a sky-high estimate of $30m to $50m.

Jean-Michel Basquiat, Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads), 1983 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Evidently inspired by Leonardo da Vinci’s 1493 pen-and-ink drawing on paper A man tricked by Gypsies (also known as Five grotesque heads), from the Royal Collection Trust at Windsor Castle in London, Basquiat’s freestyle interpretation in oil stick and acrylic against a burnt orange background crackles with the artist’s terse way with wordplay and actually features eight heads in all.

Sources indicate that measuring 80in by 80in, the painting has no exhibition history, at least none acknowledged in Christie’s online catalogue entry—though it was included in the Whitney Museum of American Art’s 1992 Basquiat retrospective. The catalogue entry for the Whitney exhibition listed the owner as Zurich’s Bruno Bischofberger, an early and important champion of the artist. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s London in October 2005, when it was the top lot at £736,000 ($1.3m) including fees against an estimate of £400,000 to £600,000. Sotheby’s at the time identified the buyer as “US Trade” and the current consignor acquired it from that entity in 2006.

Julia Jo, One Fell Swoop, 2026 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

The evening ended on a sweet note with Julia Jo’s large-scale abstraction One Fell Swoop (2026), donated to benefit the Newly introduced York-based Coalition for the Homeless. It set a new auction record for Jo’s work, fetching $320,000 ($409,600 with fees). (The night’s other new auction record was for the work of the Spanish artist Antonio Santín.).

Apart from that feeling, the outlook was not as rosy. “It’s been a very long week, with a lot of art, and I think people are tired,” DeLuca said. “The theme of the week is that estimates are a little aspirational.”.

The long week’s last burst of activity will be a pair of day sales at Christie’s on Friday (20 November), after which the US art industry will mark a pause to observe Thanksgiving before migrating south for Art Basel Miami Beach.

GTA 6 has become a cultural reference point far beyond its medium. Tapping into that can allow non-endemic brands to be part of the biggest entertainment event of the year. if they can forge a memorable and meaningful connection to the release, that is.

It has been revealed that A lot of the posts on social media smacked of lazy bandwagon jumping, and gamers have been quick to call that out. Quick tip: adding "Grand Theft" before your own brand name might reveal more than what you intended about your value proposition.

#92064. Latest Update: DxO Year in Review 2026: Four New Versions and Where Each One Fits in Your Edit

Latest Update: DxO Year in Review 2026: Four New Versions and Where Each One Fits in Your Edit

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2872 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A lot changed in DxO’s photo editing tools in 2026.
  • Together, DxO’s software updates changed how a hard file gets edited, from first cleanup to finished look.
  • In a recent development, full disclosureThis article was brought to you by DxO.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A lot changed in DxO’s photo editing tools in 2026. The strongest noise reduction reached far more cameras. Masks learned to find each person in a frame, and the distance behind them, without a brush. The glow of film around a streetlight went from a stack of layers to a single filter.

Together, DxO’s software updates changed how a hard file gets edited, from first cleanup to finished look.

In a recent development, full disclosureThis article was brought to you by DxO. DxO’s Black Friday prices apply to new licenses and upgrades of PhotoLab 10, Nik Collection 9, ViewPoint 6, PureRAW 6 and FilmPack 8 through November 29. The prices are applied automatically at dxo.com/bf26/PetaPixel, with no code required.

Photos taken in New Mexico by Chris Niccolls and Michael Bonocore, in Cuba and Morocco by Michael Bonocore, and the Milky Way by Matt Suess.

DxO released new versions of four applications in 2026: PureRAW 6, Nik Collection 9, PhotoLab 10 and, in October, ViewPoint 6. DxO keeps improving its applications, and three of them received free updates in November.

Recent findings suggest that each one handles a different stage of an edit. PureRAW cleans the RAW file, the unprocessed data a camera’s sensor records. PhotoLab develops that file into a share-worthy photograph, ViewPoint corrects perspective and distortion, and Nik Collection adds the finishing look.

Sources indicate that always looking for new ways to edit old photos, I ran photos from New Mexico, Cuba and Morocco through three of them for PetaPixel stories throughout 2026. Even though I also shoot astrophotography, a fourth story followed OM SYSTEM ambassador Matt Suess through a Milky Way edit, as he is a much more impressive editor than I am. What follows runs in the order of a typical edit of mine, and that starts before any creative decision, with the RAW file itself.

Sources indicate that if you zoom to 100% on a frame shot at a high ISO, the camera’s sensitivity setting, the flaws become obvious. There is grainy noise in the shadows, edges the lens left soft and a dust spot or two from the sensor. Every later editing adjustment that you add only makes the problems worse, and they follow the photograph through the rest of the edit.

PureRAW 6 helps to make all of these fixes. It applies noise reduction, lens corrections and dust removal to the RAW file before editing starts, then hands back a new file to edit. The usual choice for that file is a DNG, a format that keeps a RAW file’s editing flexibility. The original RAW file is never modified.

This year’s PureRAW 6 expanded the reach of DeepPRIME XD3, the stronger of PureRAW’s two noise reduction engines.

Industry observers note that in the past, it only worked with Fujifilm’s X-Trans sensors. It now works with Bayer sensors, the design used by Canon, Nikon, Sony and OM SYSTEM.

The lens corrections are an especially strong feature of DxO software, starting with PureRAW. They test each supported camera and lens pairing in their own lab, and PureRAW applies that impressive data for the exact combination that made the photograph.

In this day and age with skyrocketing storage costs, PureRAW 6 shrinks the files with a fresh DNG option called High-Fidelity Compression. In one example, a 57.8MB RAW file becomes a 136MB DNG without compression and a 17.2MB DNG with it.

I have come to find that most photographers are like me, and they often shoot with less than spotless equipment. Luckily, dust spots are automatically detected and removed across a whole batch. And in PureRAW 6, batch edits finish quicker, because the processor prepares the next image while the graphics card renders the current one.

Sources indicate that for noise reduction, start with DeepPRIME 3 and switch to XD3 for high-ISO files, heavy crops and fine detail such as feathers and fur. XD3 takes roughly twice as long, though the gap narrows on newer graphics cards, and it can leave artifacts (visible processing errors) on smooth surfaces. For portraits and architecture, stay with DeepPRIME 3.

Recent findings suggest that if the processed file goes back to Lightroom, make sure to turn off its own lens corrections and noise reduction for that file. PureRAW has already applied both, and running them a second time doubles the correction and creates artifacts.

It has been revealed that pureRAW fits a photographer who intends to keep editing in Lightroom, Photoshop or Capture One, because it only changes the file those editors receive. A photographer who would rather work in one application gets DxO’s processing inside PhotoLab 10, the tech giant’s all-in-one editor. The full walkthrough, with recommended starting values for each control, is in DxO PureRAW 6: The Ultimate Beginner’s Guide.

Brightening one face in a group photograph is a small change. Telling the software which pixels belong to that face is the slow part. The area an adjustment affects is called a mask, and building one by hand means painting an outline and then cleaning up its edges.

Industry observers note that photoLab 10 builds those masks itself, and my guide highlights each one at work on my photographs from Morocco. Its AI Masks recognize the individual people in a photograph instead of treating the group as one subject. One easy step generates a separate mask for each selected person.

For portraits the masks go finer, selecting facial skin, eyes, teeth, lips or facial hair without a hand-painted outline.

Recent findings suggest that no matter the subject matter, every photograph has depth, and the latest Depth Masks select areas by how far they are from the camera. PhotoLab builds a depth map, a model of which parts of the scene are near and which are far, without needing depth data recorded in the file.

According to recent reports, these masks utilize DxO’s own AI, which runs on the photographer’s own computer, so the masks work on an airplane or in a hotel with unreliable Wi-Fi. Additionally, for those concerned with privacy, this means that the photos are never sent to the cloud and stay local on their computer.

It has been revealed that an automatic mask is a starting point to refine. When one misses part of the subject, PhotoLab 10 lets you correct it instead of rebuilding it.

Sources indicate that their U Point technology selects pixels by comparing their color and brightness. The Control Brush applies that matching inside an area the photographer paints.

Recent findings suggest that color grading shifts the color of the shadows, midtones and highlights separately. PhotoLab 10 puts all three on a single wheel, with a Global control for the whole image.

According to recent reports, with the three ranges selected, dragging one marker moves all of them and keeps the same distance between them. This allows for trying a different color direction without rebuilding the color grade.

The free 10.3 upgrade, released in November, extends the masks to noise reduction. Each local adjustment, an edit confined to a masked area, can now use its own noise reduction engine. Reserve DeepPRIME XD3 for the subject, where it extracts the most detail, and let DeepPRIME 3 handle the rest of the frame.

Point a camera up at a building and its walls lean toward each other in the frame. That is a perspective problem, and no exposure or color control fixes it. ViewPoint 6 is the application to fix that: it corrects geometry, perspective and distortion.

According to recent reports, released in October, it adds AI masks to ReShape Fusion, the tool that reshapes part of a picture. A mask finds the outline of a subject, however complex its shape, and the correction mesh is built to match it.

In a recent development, the photographer sets how far the change carries into the rest of the picture. As before, the correction needs no forced crop.

According to recent reports, the standalone app now opens RAW files directly. November’s 6.1 patch adds DNG export, so a RAW file corrected in ViewPoint can leave with its geometry fixed and continue in any editor that opens DNG files.

In a recent development, saving and exporting are now separate. Save records the corrections for the next session, and Export produces the finished image.

Photographers miss the days when film made bright lights glow. Light passed through the film’s layers, bounced off the back and leaked in again, leaving a soft halo around streetlights and candle flames. A digital sensor records the same lights with crisp edges and no halo.

Rebuilding that glow in Photoshop means duplicating the image, blurring the copy, masking the highlights and blending the layers together. Nik Collection 9 does it with one filter. The suite is a set of plug-ins for Photoshop, Lightroom Classic, Affinity and PhotoLab, and every application in the suite can open the photo from inside one of those editors.

That filter, Halation, is one of three new effects in version 9, each shown on my photographs from Cuba in my Nik Collection 9 guide. It works best on an image that already has strong highlights worth softening, such as a night cityscape or a backlit portrait.

Chromatic Shift copies the color offset of a misaligned printing press, the red edge on one side of a face and the blue-green shadow on the other. A subtle shift of that kind gives a portrait a retro, editorial feel. Using an AI mask can keep it off the eyes and lips.

Glass Effect distorts the frame as if it were shot through textured glass. On a portrait, the distortion can wrap the frame while an AI Object Mask keeps the face sharp.

Sources indicate that the new Color Grading filter in Color Efex, one of the Nik Collection 9’s plug-ins, puts shadows, midtones, and highlights on one wheel. Two shortcuts move all three together: one shifts hue, the color the tones lean toward, and the other shifts saturation, how vivid that color is. It gives photographers who finish in Photoshop, Lightroom Classic or Affinity the single-wheel grading that PhotoLab 10 has built in.

According to recent reports, eighteen blending modes now sit inside Color Efex and a second plug-in, Analog Efex. A blending mode sets how an effect mixes with the image beneath it. On the Halation filter, Multiply sinks the glow into the shadows for a darker image, while Soft Light keeps the glow and more of the original contrast.

Aim any of these effects at part of the frame with AI Object Masks and Depth Masks, which work in every plug-in.

It has been revealed that version 9.2, the November update, adds snapshots. A snapshot saves every edit made so far. Try a different look, then come back to the snapshot at any point in the session.

The update also brings 18 new presets, or saved looks: six each for Color Efex, Analog Efex and Silver Efex.

Industry observers note that matt Suess has photographed dark skies for decades and leads astrophotography workshops in places such as Grand Teton National Park. One of the most challenging files he has edited came from a test.

He normally caps his Milky Way exposures at ISO 6400, but he wanted to test PureRAW, so he shot a nightscape at ISO 12,800 to see how far he could push it.

Sharpening or adding contrast to a noisy night file bakes the noise in, so Suess runs noise reduction before he develops the RAW file. He opens PureRAW’s Preview and Process mode, which demonstrates the controls first, because a night sky is where he wants to make those calls himself.

Sources indicate that XD3 is the stronger engine, but a star field is where Suess often skips it. That much processing can start to soften the stars themselves, so he picks DeepPRIME 3, and he treats it as a per-image call.

He keeps Lens Sharpness on Standard, since the Hard setting starts sharpening the noise along with everything else.

The develop pass in Lightroom stays restrained. Suess switches to a color profile built for landscapes in place of the flatter default, adds a little contrast and holds back on the other sliders. He treats this pass as the place to protect the sky’s real color, with the finishing touches saved for later.

According to recent reports, the finish happens in the Nik Collection 9 plug-in Color Efex, with the same four filters in the same order on nearly every Milky Way photograph. ClearView lifts the faint gray haze that dulls a night photo, and Suess keeps it low so it does not outline the stars. Glamour Glow spreads a soft bloom of light from the brightest points.

Remove Color Cast pulls one unwanted color out of the frame. Tonal Contrast raises contrast separately in the shadows, midtones and highlights, and he raises the midtones, where the structure of the Milky Way sits. Once the stack works, he saves it as a preset for the next photograph from his astrophotography session.

Suess fine tunes the filters with two tools. A Color Mask, a local adjustment added inside a filter, selects one color across the whole frame. He uses it on air glow, the faint green tint that indicates in the sky on very dark nights.

An AI Object Mask points a filter at a single foreground element instead of the whole image.

Industry observers note that he judges every move at 100%, not from the small preview. Each one gets a before and after comparison, and he looks for halos, the bright rings that too much contrast leaves around stars. Every step of the edit, with his settings, is in How to Turn a Flat, Noisy RAW Into a Finished Milky Way Photograph.

Some jobs cannot be done by developing a RAW file: a layered composite, added text, an object removed or replaced, detailed retouching. Those jobs need a pixel editor, software that changes the pixels of the picture directly.

It has been revealed that dxO declared a partnership with Affinity by Canva in September. Affinity runs on macOS and Windows and costs nothing beyond a free Canva account.

Sources indicate that photoLab 10 launched without a direct Export to Affinity button, and PhotoLab 10.1 added it. With the 10.3 update, Affinity’s own .af files appear in PhotoLab’s library like JPEG and TIFF files.

That makes a round trip possible. A photographer can develop a RAW file in PhotoLab, continue in Affinity with retouching, compositing or layout, then finish and export the result in PhotoLab. Changes saved in Affinity are visible in PhotoLab straight away, and PhotoLab’s own adjustments are stored separately and never change the Affinity document.

Nik Collection 9.2 connects from the other side by saving its work as an .af file. The file keeps the edited image and the original as separate layers, and the masks come across as layers too. Going the other way has a limit: Nik Collection opens an .af file with its layers merged into a single image.

DxO’s Black Friday prices cover upcoming licenses and upgrades of their five applications through November 29th, 2026. They apply to purchases from dxo.com/bf26/PetaPixel for macOS and Windows, are applied automatically with no code required, and cannot be combined with any other offers.

It has been revealed that pureRAW 6 suits a photographer who wants cleaner files and looks to keep editing in Lightroom, Photoshop or Capture One. It is $99.99, down from $139.99. The upgrade from version 4 or 5 is $69.99, down from $89.99.

PhotoLab 10 suits a photographer who wants one application for the whole edit, with DxO’s processing, the automatic masks and the Color Grading wheel in the same place. It is $199.99, down from $249.99. The upgrade from version 8 or 9 is $99.99, down from $129.99.

According to recent reports, nik Collection 9 suits a photographer who has an editor already and wants the finishing looks: film glow, color grading and blending modes without stacked layers. It is $149.99, down from $179.99. The upgrade from version 7 or 8 is $79.99, down from $99.99.

ViewPoint 6 corrects geometry, perspective and distortion, and version 6, released in October, adds an AI mask that fits a correction to the outline of a subject. It is $99.99, down from $129.99. The upgrade from version 5 is $69.99, down from $84.99.

It has been revealed that filmPack 8 recreates the look of classic film stocks from laboratory measurements of real film, and it includes a tool that prepares home-scanned negatives and slides for editing. It is $74.99, down from $149.99. The upgrade from version 7 is $49.99, down from $89.99.

It has been revealed that free trials of every DxO application are available from dxo.com. November’s 10.3, 9.2 and 6.1 updates are free for owners of PhotoLab 10, Nik Collection 9 and ViewPoint 6.
